content: Certainly. In 2010, China failed to meet either of the two established benchmarks, and as a result, the standard was not achieved. In India, the under-five mortality rate in 2010 was 63 per 1,000 live births. Out-of-pocket health expenditures accounted for 61% of the total health expenditures. India did not meet either of the two benchmarks, and therefore, the standard was not satisfied. In Kenya, the under-five mortality rate in 2010 was 85 per 1,000 live births, and out-of-pocket health expenditures constituted 43% of the total health expenditures. Kenya also failed to meet either of the two benchmarks, and thus, the standard was not achieved. In the Netherlands, the under-five mortality rate in 2010 was 4 per 1,000 live births, and out-of-pocket health expenditures were only 5% of the total health expenditures. The Netherlands successfully met both benchmarks, thereby achieving the standard. In South Africa, the under-five mortality rate in 2010 was 57 per 1,000 live births, while out-of-pocket health expenditures accounted for 17% of the total health expenditures. South Africa met the second benchmark but fell significantly short of meeting the first benchmark. Consequently, the standard was not achieved. In Thailand, the under-five mortality rate in 2010 was 13 per 1,000 live births, and out-of-pocket health expenditures were 14% of the total health expenditures. Thailand met the second benchmark but narrowly missed the first. While it came very close, the standard was only partially achieved. In the United Kingdom, the under-five mortality rate in 2010 was 5 per 1,000 live births, and out-of-pocket health expenditures were 10% of the total health expenditures. The UK met both benchmarks and successfully achieved the standard. In the United States of America, the under-five mortality rate in 2010 was 8 per 1,000 live births, and out-of-pocket health expenditures were 12% of the total health expenditures. The USA satisfied both benchmarks and met the standard. Rationale for Standards and Benchmarks: There is significant variability in the coverage and quality of cause-of-death data across countries. High coverage and accurate information on tuberculosis (TB)-related deaths are critical for monitoring the magnitude, distribution, and trends of the TB burden. This data is also essential for informing policy decisions and allocating resources effectively. Mortality attributable to TB can be directly measured in countries with robust vital registration systems that have high coverage and accurate cause-of-death coding. However, the number of deaths among patients undergoing TB treatment is not an accurate measure of TB mortality, as it includes deaths from all causes and excludes TB-related deaths among individuals not registered for treatment. Low coverage of TB death registration can lead to underreporting of mortality. Additionally, a high proportion of ill-defined causes of death can result in inaccurate estimates of TB mortality distribution, hindering effective resource allocation. Coverage is defined as the number of deaths reported in a given year as a percentage of the estimated deaths in the resident population of a country. The quality of data within a vital registration system is determined by the proportion of deaths assigned to ICD codes for symptoms, signs, and ill-defined conditions (ICD-9 codes 780–799 and ICD-10 codes R00–R99). These criteria are based on WHO quality standards for vital registration data. To meet the standard, both benchmarks must be satisfied: 1. Cause of death must be documented in at least 90% of total recorded deaths in either a national or sample vital registration system. 2. Less than 10% of deaths should have ICD codes for ill-defined causes. If only one benchmark is satisfied, the standard is considered partially met. If neither benchmark is satisfied, the standard is not met. Recommended Actions: Although vital registration systems often fall outside the direct control of National TB Programs (NTPs), they remain within the sphere of influence of these programs. TB program directors should use assessment results as evidence to advocate for changes in other sectors to improve the accuracy of TB burden measurement. If a high-quality vital registration system does not exist, alternative methods such as sample vital registration systems, mortality surveys, or demographic surveillance systems using verbal autopsy can serve as interim solutions to improve TB mortality estimates. Financial plans for TB surveillance activities should consider investments in these areas. Example from Thailand: A study in Thailand used the Health Metrics Network tool, combined with systems analysis and literature review, to evaluate the collection and flow of mortality and cause-of-death data. Based on the Survey of Population Change, a nationally representative household survey conducted every decade, the coverage of vital registration of deaths in Thailand was determined to be 95%. However, approximately 40% of deaths were classified as ill-defined. Based on these findings, the standard would have been partially met. Recommendations for improvement included training physicians and data coders, harmonizing death certificates and registries, and increasing public awareness of the importance of registering all deaths. Surveillance of Drug-Resistant TB: Monitoring drug-resistant TB is essential for understanding TB epidemiology, analyzing trends, assessing NTP performance, forecasting treatment needs, designing standardized treatment regimens, and responding promptly to outbreaks. Failure to monitor drug-resistant TB contributes to poor treatment outcomes and the transmission of resistant strains in the community. Surveillance systems based on routine diagnostic testing of previously untreated TB cases are the preferred approach for monitoring drug resistance. Alternatively, special surveys of representative samples of previously untreated TB cases can be conducted in settings with limited laboratory capacity. The quality of drug susceptibility testing (DST) results should be assured by a Supranational TB Reference Laboratory (SRL). To meet the standard, at least one of the following benchmarks must be satisfied: 1. Rifampicin susceptibility status (positive/negative) must be documented for at least 75% of new pulmonary TB cases. 2. Rifampicin susceptibility status must be documented for a nationally representative drug resistance survey of new pulmonary TB cases. If neither benchmark is satisfied, the standard is not met. If rifampicin susceptibility status is documented for 50–74% of new pulmonary TB cases, or if a nationally representative drug resistance survey is underway, the standard is partially met. Example from Latvia: In Latvia, an electronic TB surveillance information system was used to assess whether minimal data elements were captured for previously untreated TB cases. Of the 703 previously untreated pulmonary TB cases reported in 2011, 579 had a positive culture, and among them, 562 had available DST results for rifampicin (80%). The concordance for rifampicin in the most recent proficiency testing conducted with the SRL was ≥95%. The standard was considered met in Latvia because the first benchmark was satisfied.
